title: Xi Jinping Lands in Washington as Trump Tries to Lock In a Fragile Trade Truce
dek: China's leader arrived for his first state visit to Washington since 2015, with tariffs, rare earths and artificial intelligence all on the table as a one-year trade truce winds down.
body: Xi Jinping touched down on American soil Wednesday, kicking off a three-day state visit that Beijing is already spinning as a diplomatic triumph. According to the schedule announced by the White House, <cite index="19-8,19-9">Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan arrived at Andrews Air Force Base on September 23, with Trump greeting the couple at the airport and holding a welcoming ceremony.</cite> A full state dinner follows Thursday, with <cite index="19-10,19-11">Trump greeting Xi and Peng at the White House, followed by a guard of honor review in the Rose Garden before the summit meeting, and a state dinner that evening in the East Room, attended by several heads of American technology companies.</cite>

This is no small photo-op. <cite index="23-4">The trip marks Xi's first state visit to Washington since 2015 and his second face-to-face meeting this year with Trump, as the world's two largest economies try to stabilize a relationship strained by trade, technology and national security disputes.</cite> China's foreign ministry, never shy about stagecraft, is framing the reciprocal visits as something bigger than routine diplomacy. Spokesman Guo Jiakun said the exchanges of visits by the two presidents within six months mark <cite index="27-5">"a milestone of historic significance."</cite>

The Rampart's view: Americans should welcome any deal that gets Beijing to play fair on trade, but they should be clear-eyed about who has spent decades gaming the system. Just days before Xi's arrival, <cite index="19-5">Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng met with US Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in New York City, where they agreed to set up an AI dialogue.</cite> That's fine as far as it goes — but an "AI dialogue" is not the same as enforceable protections for American workers, American factories and American intellectual property. Communist China did not become the world's manufacturing superpower by playing by the rules; it did it in no small part by hollowing out the American industrial base while Washington's bipartisan establishment cheered "free trade" from the sidelines.

The stakes go well beyond ceremony. <cite index="24-1">The visit comes with a one-year trade truce winding down</cite>, meaning the tariffs, export controls and rare-earth mineral restrictions that have defined the Trump administration's China policy are all back in play. Rare earths in particular remain a glaring vulnerability — American manufacturers, defense contractors and automakers still depend heavily on Chinese-controlled supply chains for materials essential to everything from fighter jets to electric vehicle batteries. If this summit produces anything less than real, verifiable concessions on that front, it will be another missed opportunity to bring critical supply chains home.

To be fair to the administration, this is a very different posture than the accommodation of past presidents. Trump has shown a willingness to use tariffs as leverage rather than treat access to American markets as an entitlement, and his aides insist the summit is about "managing differences," not papering over them. Critics on the left and inside the foreign policy establishment will no doubt argue that engagement and rapprochement with Beijing serve global stability and that confrontation risks economic disruption — a view that deserves a hearing even if it underestimates how badly American workers have already paid for decades of one-sided globalization.

What happens in the Rose Garden and the East Room this week will shape the U.S.-China relationship for the rest of Trump's term. The Rampart will be watching for one thing above all: whether the president walks away with real, enforceable commitments that put American workers and American sovereignty first — or another round of vague promises dressed up as a historic breakthrough.

title: Trump Admin Tells Congress Nearly All 2027 Refugees Will Be Afrikaners Fleeing South Africa
dek: The administration's notice to Congress caps refugee admissions at 17,500 for fiscal 2027, with the program almost entirely reoriented toward white South Africans who say they face land seizures and persecution.
body: For years the U.S. refugee program operated as an all-purpose entry point for people fleeing conflicts from every corner of the globe, admitted with little scrutiny of who was actually coming or whether they'd assimilate. This week, the Trump administration made official just how thoroughly it has reshaped that system. <cite index="29-2">The Trump administration plans to limit the number of refugees admitted to the country in 2027 to 17,500 mostly white South Africans, the administration told Congress Tuesday, as it continues to transform a program that at one point served as a pathway to safety for people fleeing war and strife from countries around the world.</cite>

The administration's reasoning, laid out in its formal notice, centers on land seizures and discrimination faced by Afrikaner farmers. <cite index="29-3">In a notice to Congress obtained by The Associated Press, the administration said the white South Africans faced seizures of their land and other forms of persecution and would be likely to assimilate when they come to America.</cite> The State Department's language was blunt about priorities, stating admissions will <cite index="32-6">"primarily be Afrikaners from South Africa,"</cite> and predicting that <cite index="32-7">"The United States anticipates that Afrikaners from South Africa will fully assimilate into the United States in a manner that preserves taxpayer resources for U.S."</cite> citizens and existing refugee communities.

This is precisely the kind of selective, merit-and-outcomes-based approach to immigration that voters have been demanding for years — a program that asks not just "is this person fleeing something bad" but "will this person actually integrate, work and contribute rather than become a permanent drain on taxpayers." For too long the refugee system function as an open-ended commitment with no serious accounting of assimilation outcomes. Whatever one thinks of the specific group chosen, the underlying principle — that America gets to decide who it admits and on what terms — is not radical. It's sovereignty.

The scale of the shift is dramatic. <cite index="32-8">The administration increased the refugee cap for South Africans earlier this year to 17,500 from a limit of 7,500 for all refugees, informing Congress of the change through an emergency determination.</cite> That means a program that once spread admissions across dozens of nationalities and crisis zones is now, in practice, a single-country pipeline. Background on the population in question: <cite index="29-7">Afrikaners are the descendants of mainly Dutch and French colonial settlers who first arrived in South Africa in the 17th century.</cite>

Predictably, the policy has drawn fire from refugee advocates and the South African government alike. <cite index="29-4">The South African government has repeatedly rejected the idea that the white South Africans, who are Afrikaners, are a persecuted minority in the home country.</cite> Refugee advocacy groups go further, arguing the administration <cite index="30-4">has excluded vulnerable populations worldwide</cite> by narrowing the program so severely, while South African officials have <cite index="30-5">strongly denied claims of White genocide.</cite> These are legitimate criticisms that deserve to be weighed: a refugee system this narrow inevitably leaves out people facing documented violence and war elsewhere in the world, and the administration's underlying persecution claims remain sharply contested by the very government whose citizens are in question.

CNN reporting also notes the program hasn't been without friction even for its intended beneficiaries — the outlet found the shift <cite index="32-9">has sparked diplomatic spats, prompted a scramble to open a processing site in South Africa, generated highly unusual requests from applicants and produced high denial rates, due in part to criminal records among some applicants</cite>. That's a reminder that even a dramatically scaled-back, selective refugee program requires competent execution — something this administration, like every administration before it, will be judged on in the months ahead.

title: Harris Parachutes Into Michigan to Prop Up Progressive Senate Nominee El-Sayed
dek: The former vice president joined Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit as national Democrats scramble to unify a fractured party ahead of a toss-up race against Trump-endorsed Mike Rogers.
body: Six weeks from a midterm election that could decide control of the Senate, Democrats are sending in their most recognizable — and most politically damaged — messenger. <cite index="50-2">Former Vice President Kamala Harris on Tuesday made her first major midterm foray, traveling to Michigan to boost Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's Senate bid, a high-profile stop that doubled as a test of her standing as a potential 2028 contender.</cite> The pair appeared together at a Detroit-area roundtable, where <cite index="50-3">participants highlighted Black women dying at three to four times the rate of white women in connection with childbirth</cite> and how the race could shape federal health policy.

The optics of the reunion are awkward, to put it gently. El-Sayed is no natural Harris ally — <cite index="53-4">Abdul led the Uncommitted Movement against Kamala Harris in 2024</cite>, a protest campaign that dogged her presidential run over the administration's handling of the Israel-Hamas war. Republican nominee Mike Rogers wasted no time pointing that out, releasing a statement calling the pairing <cite index="53-3">"Desperate times call for desperate measures, and Abdul is so desperate that he's parachuting Kamala Harris into Michigan to save his flailing campaign."</cite>

The race matters well beyond Michigan. <cite index="52-7">If Democrats hold the seat, which was opened by Sen. Gary Peters' announced retirement, they'd still need to win at least four more currently held by Republicans to flip the chamber.</cite> El-Sayed, a doctor by training, is running well to the left of the party's establishment wing — <cite index="52-13">El-Sayed is running to the left of the Democratic Party establishment, including advocating for universal healthcare</cite> — and would make history if he wins: <cite index="9-4">El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate, faces Republican former congressman Mike Rogers for the seat.</cite>

The unity effort papers over real cracks. El-Sayed's bruising primary against Rep. Haley Stevens split the party's coalition, and <cite index="47-6">Black voters, including Anthony, largely backed Stevens</cite> over El-Sayed. Jewish Democrats in the state have voiced similar unease, with one prominent party fundraiser telling reporters that <cite index="52-10">"Jews in Michigan are currently scared"</cite> by their Senate options — a discomfort tied to El-Sayed's sharp criticism of Israel. Rogers, for his part, <cite index="47-7">has openly appealed to Black Democrats as well as Jewish voters</cite>, sensing an opening in the very fractures Harris flew in to smooth over.

From The Rampart's vantage point, this is what happens when a party lets its activist base pick nominees rather than candidates who can actually govern for the whole state. Michigan voters who backed Trump twice are being asked to send a self-described progressive who ran against his own party's presidential nominee to the U.S. Senate for six years — while the same Beltway figures who lost Michigan in 2024 fly in to vouch for him. That's not a coalition; it's a reunion tour for a losing message.

Democrats and El-Sayed's supporters would counter that the enthusiasm gap cuts the other way — that grassroots energy, not establishment credentials, is what wins tough races, and that El-Sayed's focus on health care and maternal mortality speaks directly to kitchen-table concerns Rogers has largely ignored. There is polling to back at least part of that claim, with one recent survey showing <cite index="49-6">El-Sayed's lead over Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's U.S. Senate race widening six weeks before Election Day.</cite> Whether that lead holds up once the Uncommitted Movement history and the Israel controversy get more airtime remains the central question of the race.

body: Lonnie G. Bunch III, the 14th secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, announced on September 8 that he will retire at the end of 2026. The Board of Regents has launched a national search and has not named a successor.

"It is with very mixed emotions and heartfelt gratitude that I announce my retirement," Bunch said. He told NPR that the president's criticism of the Smithsonian wasn't part of his decision, while stressing the institution's independence. "The work we do explains the complexity of America," he said.

The conflict has been building for more than a year. In August 2025, President Trump called for a "comprehensive internal review" of eight Smithsonian museums and directed them to "celebrate American exceptionalism." In July 2026, the administration released a report accusing the National Museum of American History of "extreme political activism."

Bunch has had a historic career. He was the Smithsonian's first historian and first Black secretary, and he founded the National Museum of African American History and Culture. That record deserves respect, and so do the difficult chapters of American history the museums hold.

The populist complaint was never about telling hard truths. It was about tone. Families who paid for these institutions with their taxes walked through exhibits that seemed more interested in indicting the country than explaining how it became the freest and most prosperous nation in history. Complexity and pride can exist side by side.

The next secretary should be judged on whether a kid from Milwaukee or Midland leaves the Mall more proud of being American and better informed about the country's history. Critics warn that political pressure on museums threatens scholarly independence. The Regents' choice will show which view wins.
dek: The Smithsonian's secretary is retiring at year's end after a year of clashes with the White House over how its museums present the nation's history.

title: Bunch's Exit Gives the Smithsonian a Chance to Tell America's Story With Pride Again

body: President Trump said Monday that his envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, met with an Iranian delegation for three hours on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, and that the meeting "went very well."

Trump told reporters that another session is planned for the "very near future" and framed the choice facing Tehran in stark terms: "It's potential greatness, or obliteration." He said Iran "wants to talk to us" and that "the relationship is developing."
The president also said he expects to sign an agreement "right after" the November midterm elections. Asked about the talks, Witkoff said he felt "very good right now."

For voters who backed Trump on a promise of strength without endless foreign entanglements, this is the test: pressure first, then a deal that puts American interests ahead of the globalist consensus that shaped past Iran agreements. The details, which the White House has not released, will decide whether that promise holds.

Critics will note that the war with Iran remains one of the issues weighing on voters heading into November, and that a deal timed to land after Election Day spares the administration from having its terms judged at the ballot box.

Also Monday, Trump met British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, where he said he was unfamiliar with the UK's decision to sanction Israeli settlements, although officials had reportedly briefed him on it beforehand.
dek: Witkoff and Kushner met an Iranian delegation at the UN General Assembly. The president says a deal could come right after the midterms.

body: Customs and Border Protection says it has now gone 16 straight months without releasing a single migrant into the country at the southern border, the kind of number that was unthinkable during the surge years.

Apprehensions fell 5 percent from July to August, according to a monthly roundup of federal data. Of those caught, 88 percent were single adults and 64 percent were Mexican citizens. Rio Grande Valley in South Texas remained the busiest sector.

Enforcement capacity is growing. Border Patrol has more than 2,200 trainees in its academy, the largest cadre in its history, and plans a new 87-acre station near Tucson. The U.S. military has shot down about 300 suspected cartel drones this year, and cartel drone activity reportedly fell 75 percent after laser systems were deployed alongside 800 Mexican troops.

Wall construction is facing resistance. On September 14 a coalition of 230 landowners in the Big Bend region filed the sixth lawsuit challenging the federal waivers used to speed up construction, citing ranches, river access and family graves. In Arizona's San Rafael Valley, three protesters were arrested September 15 at a construction site.

The administration's supporters see the numbers as proof that the border was always a question of will, not resources. Opponents point to other costs in the same reporting: overcrowded detention sites, deportations to third countries such as Equatorial Guinea, and an ICE whistleblower alleging lowered hiring standards.
The legal fights in Texas are the ones to watch. Private property rights matter to conservatives too, and how the government handles the Big Bend landowners will shape how durable the wall is.
dek: August apprehensions fell another 5 percent, and Border Patrol is training its largest academy class ever. Landowners in Big Bend are suing over the wall.

body: The George W. Bush Institute published its September immigration update on Monday. Its conclusion is meant as a warning: current policies will cut legal immigration by 33 to 50 percent by the end of President Trump's second term, meaning 1.5 million to 2.4 million fewer legal immigrants.

The report, by immigration policy director Laura Collins, lists the changes. Refugee admissions totaled 10,258 in the first ten months of fiscal 2026, compared with 38,102 for all of fiscal 2025. Student visa issuance fell 23 percent in 2025, and F-1 visas fell 33.4 percent. Naturalization applications dropped 74 percent this year.
Its figure of the month is $103,265, the proposed fee for most new H-1B applications for skilled foreign workers.

From the populist side, much of this list reads as a scorecard of promises kept. H-1B visas have long been used to replace American tech workers with cheaper labor, and a six-figure fee forces employers to prove they can't hire here first. Lower overall numbers are what the voters who elected this administration asked for.

The report also points to problems that aren't a matter of ideology. USCIS has a record 12.1 million pending cases while processing fewer applications than in any year in over a decade, and the employment-based green card backlog exceeds 1.2 million. A system that lets people wait forever is not an immigration policy. Whatever the number of admissions, the agency should decide cases quickly.
Business groups and the Bush Institute argue the cuts will cost the economy workers and talent. That debate will keep going through November. The immigration restriction side is winning it for now.
dek: A new report projects 1.5 to 2.4 million fewer legal immigrants by the end of Trump's term, and puts the proposed H-1B fee at $103,265.

body: Election Day is November 3, and Republicans are defending narrow majorities in both the House and the Senate. That margin is thin enough that a small drop in base turnout could hand Democrats the gavel.

NPR reports that a Senate map once seen as friendly to Republicans has become competitive, with races in Iowa, Texas, Ohio and Alaska in play. In Texas, Republican nominee Ken Paxton faces Democrat James Talarico. The Washington Post reported last week that Democrats feel increasingly confident about taking control of Congress.

Voters' concerns cover the war in Iran, immigration, tariffs, gas prices and the overall cost of living. NPR also reports that the president's approval ratings are at record lows and that voters see a gap between their priorities and the White House's.

For the America First movement, the lesson is not to turn away from the border and trade fights that won in 2024, but to connect them to the kitchen table. Fewer workers competing for jobs, tariffs that bring factories home, and energy that lowers prices at the pump are the argument. Candidates who make it clearly will outrun the polls.

Democrats are betting affordability decides the election and that their voters are more motivated. Polls have favored them on the House. The next six weeks will show whether Republicans can close that gap.
dek: Senate races in Iowa, Texas, Ohio and Alaska have turned competitive, and Democrats are feeling bullish. Turnout among the base will decide it.
